lectures.title: Blockchain in Geopolitical Competition - lesson slides
Blockchain in Geopolitical Competition - assigned reading

questions.question_stem: A government loses access to major foreign payment networks and cannot easily move reserves or settle cross-border transactions. Which concept best explains why this is a sovereignty problem rather than only a banking inconvenience?
questions.correct_answer: Financial rails are strategic infrastructure because they determine who can move value, settle obligations, and withstand pressure.
incorrect_answers: Financial rails are commercial utilities because they mostly improve bank efficiency without changing state capacity under pressure.
Foreign reserves are accounting assets because reported balances matter more than the ability to mobilize them through settlement systems.
Payment chokepoints are technical coordination problems because domestic clearing systems can usually substitute for foreign network access.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames payment and settlement access as a form of state power. Losing access can weaken reserve mobility, trade settlement, and resilience under geopolitical pressure.

questions.question_stem: A student says, "Blockchain removes governments from finance because anyone can transact on a public chain." What is the strongest correction?
questions.correct_answer: Blockchain can reduce some legacy chokepoints while creating new control points around ledgers, exchanges, issuers, custodians, and service providers.
incorrect_answers: Blockchain shifts control mainly to miners or validators, so governments can address financial risks by regulating consensus participants alone.
Blockchain makes enforcement depend mostly on smart-contract code, so policy concerns are settled at the protocol-design layer alone in practice.
Blockchain reduces bank involvement by moving settlement to wallets, so public ledgers operate largely outside geopolitical leverage and sanctions.
questions.explanation: The lesson's central claim is redistribution of control, not automatic decentralization. Open rails can bypass some intermediaries but often depend on visible ledgers and service-layer actors that can become chokepoints.

questions.question_stem: Which policy signal most clearly fits the United States posture toward digital money?
questions.correct_answer: Favoring private digital-asset markets and regulated dollar stablecoins while resisting a federal retail CBDC.
incorrect_answers: Building a bloc-wide rulebook around digital public money to reduce dependence on foreign payment platforms in Europe.
Restricting private crypto speculation while promoting a state-observable CBDC as the preferred digital-money rail.
Discouraging private crypto with taxes while steering retail experimentation into a central-bank digital currency pilot.
questions.explanation: The United States case is described as market-led but dollar-protective: it tends to support private-sector digital assets and regulated payment stablecoins rather than a federal retail CBDC.

questions.question_stem: Why is the EU's MiCA-style rulemaking paired with digital euro exploration under an autonomy-oriented strategy?
questions.correct_answer: Both aim to reduce fragmentation and dependence by bringing digital finance under bloc-level supervision and resilient public-money infrastructure.
incorrect_answers: They rely on private dollar stablecoins to preserve cross-border liquidity while leaving most crypto oversight to national authorities.
They prioritize retail speculation and exchange growth while delaying common supervision until private markets have scaled across the bloc.
They treat digital finance mainly as a sanctions-resilience tool by routing settlement through offshore exchanges and token issuers abroad.
questions.explanation: The EU example emphasizes supervisory integration and payment autonomy. MiCA reduces internal regulatory fragmentation, while the digital euro is tied to resilience, public money, and reduced dependence on non-European platforms.

questions.question_stem: China restricts private crypto speculation while developing state-observable digital money. What broader policy logic best explains this combination?
questions.correct_answer: China is pursuing state-capacity control: digital money is acceptable when it remains observable and governable by state institutions.
incorrect_answers: China is using regulatory clarity to attract private crypto firms while leaving wallet identity and settlement rules mostly to markets.
China is relying on privately issued dollar stablecoins to expand payment access while keeping the state out of retail transaction data.
China is treating CBDC pilots as a substitute for monetary caution while tolerating broad speculative token trading in markets.
questions.explanation: The lesson stresses that China is not simply anti-digital-money. It is anti-uncontrolled digital money and favors state-directed, observable payment capacity through instruments such as e-CNY.

questions.question_stem: A sanctioned state experiments with digital settlement tools to keep foreign trade moving. Why might this strategy expand options without fully escaping pressure?
questions.correct_answer: Alternative rails may bypass some banks, but exchanges, stablecoin issuers, bridges, and enforcement coordination can recreate service-layer chokepoints.
incorrect_answers: Alternative rails matter mainly because domestic legal approval can replace correspondent banking and remove the need for foreign counterparties.
Digital assets are useful for sanctions resilience mostly when central banks hold them, because public-chain settlement is too visible for trade workarounds.
Stablecoins preserve dollar liquidity while keeping users mostly outside the reach of issuers, exchanges, brokers, and off-ramp control layers.
questions.explanation: The Russia-focused discussion shows the two-sided nature of sanctions adaptation. Digital assets can provide settlement flexibility, but practical use often depends on services and counterparties exposed to monitoring or enforcement.

questions.question_stem: Why is North Korea's crypto activity treated as a distinct geopolitical model rather than ordinary adoption or hub-building?
questions.correct_answer: It is framed as state-linked coercive revenue generation through theft, laundering, and sanctions-evasion activity.
incorrect_answers: It is framed as user-driven stablecoin adoption under inflation and weak currencies, focused on savings and transfers.
It is framed as regulated hub-building that licenses exchanges and attracts digital-asset firms under state-set market rules.
It is framed as official CBDC development aimed at domestic payment supervision and public-money modernization.
questions.explanation: The North Korea case is not presented as market adoption, formal regulatory integration, or CBDC development. It illustrates coercive extraction through theft and laundering.

questions.question_stem: India promotes digital rupee pilots while taxes, compliance burdens, and central-bank warnings create friction around private crypto. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.correct_answer: India is integrating digital finance cautiously by favoring state-approved innovation while discouraging but not simply banning private crypto activity.
incorrect_answers: India is following a U.S.-style market-led approach by centering regulated private stablecoins and rejecting official retail digital money.
India is following a China-style control model by suppressing private crypto while making the CBDC the only permitted digital rail for users.
India is treating crypto mainly as a sanctions-resilience tool by using private tokens to keep foreign trade settlement outside regulated banks and state rails.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses India to show regulated integration with monetary caution. Official digital rails are promoted while private crypto faces friction from taxes, compliance rules, and central-bank concern.
questions.lesson_block: India: Regulated Integration With Monetary Caution

questions.question_stem: A country with high inflation and weak currency sees heavy demand for dollar-like stablecoins. Which argument best explains this pattern?
questions.correct_answer: Stablecoins can become pragmatic tools for dollar access, savings, and cross-border transfer when local monetary conditions are unstable.
incorrect_answers: Stablecoins become attractive mainly because issuers conduct local monetary policy and insure holders against exchange-rate losses.
Stablecoins are used primarily as governance tokens for domestic public-finance programs when commercial banks cannot extend credit.
Stablecoin demand signals a state-led CBDC strategy because users prefer official programmable money over private dollar instruments.
questions.explanation: The Argentina and Nigeria examples show user-driven stablecoin demand under inflation, foreign-exchange pressure, and weak currency conditions. The lesson treats this as pragmatic adoption under economic pressure.
questions.lesson_block: Latin America And Sub-Saharan Africa: Pragmatic Adoption

questions.question_stem: A policymaker compares legacy bank rails, state digital rails, and open blockchain rails. Which conclusion most accurately reflects how these rails compete?
questions.correct_answer: The strategic question is which rails states trust, shape, resist, or exploit, because each rail creates different forms of dependence, visibility, scale, and control.
incorrect_answers: The main issue is choosing the rail with the lowest transaction cost, since geopolitical effects become secondary once settlement is digital and scalable.
States mainly need to decide whether CBDCs should replace private money, since public blockchains and banks converge on the same control model over time.
Rail competition is mostly a technical standards problem, because all three infrastructures expose users to similar visibility, dependence, and chokepoints in practice.
questions.explanation: The lesson closes by treating rail competition as unresolved. Legacy, state digital, and open blockchain rails coexist and compete over trust, scale, monetary hierarchy, and control points.

questions.question_stem: Why is BLOCKINT (blockchain intelligence) more than simply looking at transactions on a block explorer?
questions.correct_answer: It combines on-chain data with behavioral patterns and off-chain context such as sanctions records, law-enforcement information, filings, or open-source evidence.
incorrect_answers: It focuses on wallet clustering and token-flow tracing while treating legal records, corporate filings, and open-source evidence as separate investigative workstreams.
It treats address ownership as a cryptographic fact by using transaction signatures as direct proof of the real-world controller behind a given wallet or service account.
It relies first on private banking reports and exchange price data, using public-chain transactions mostly as background context for market activity and risk scoring.
questions.explanation: The reading distinguishes blockchain intelligence from raw tracing. BLOCKINT fuses transparent transaction data with behavioral analysis and off-chain context to support detection, attribution, and disruption.

questions.question_stem: Adversaries use crypto rails while analysts also gain durable transaction records. Which statement best captures that dual-use logic?
questions.correct_answer: Crypto can help actors move value outside some bank chokepoints, but public ledgers and service-layer dependencies can create intelligence and disruption opportunities.
incorrect_answers: Crypto gives sanctioned actors settlement flexibility mainly because public ledgers remove the need for brokers, issuers, exchanges, and off-ramp channels.
Crypto creates intelligence value mainly by replacing open transaction records with bank-style customer files held by protocol validators and wallet software.
Crypto reduces bank chokepoints, so once funds move on-chain enforcement shifts mostly to cybersecurity rather than financial disruption or service-layer regulatory pressure.
questions.explanation: TRM's argument aligns with the lesson's two-sided model: adversaries may use fast cross-border rails, but transparent ledgers, exchanges, issuers, brokers, and off-ramps can expose patterns and chokepoints.

questions.question_stem: After an enforcement action removes a named illicit marketplace, investigators see similar wallet patterns, liquidity sources, and interfaces appear under a new name. What concept does this best illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: Enforcement can displace or mutate settlement networks, so behavior and infrastructure continuity may matter more than brand names alone.
incorrect_answers: Brand changes usually break attribution because new wallet clusters and interfaces should be treated as unrelated until a court ruling.
Platform removal shows enforcement has ended the network's economic function, so later similar flows are best analyzed as fresh market activity.
Continuity under a new name mainly proves that decentralized protocols cannot be influenced by sanctions, issuers, or off-ramp controls.
questions.explanation: The reading emphasizes rebranding, displacement, and continuity under pressure. Sanctions or removals may create friction and signals, but functions can migrate to successor venues if demand and off-ramp channels remain.
